title: Service menus, add-ons and packages
audience: Mobile beauty therapists and business owners who design service menus, add-on offers and multi-visit packages
learningOutcomes: Build a service menu from the approved list, and keep every item inside the scope of the approved service
Design an add-on or package that adds volume without adding unreviewed risk or shortening required steps
Explain how the menu, the add-ons and the packages are recorded for the client and the business
referencesAtStart: Official references for this lesson: Information for registered premises and environmental health officers (updated 22 May 2026); Managing hazardous substances and irritants in the hairdressing and beauty industry (reviewed 12/09/2025).

instruction.heading: The menu is the scope, in print
instruction.body: A service menu tells the client what the business does. It is therefore a statement of scope. Every item on the menu must be on the approved service list, and every item must have been checked against the state and council rules in “Mobile beauty scope and skin-treatment boundaries”. A menu item that is not on the approved list, or that is in a category the business has not reviewed, is a scope error even if the therapist has the skill. The approved list is held in {{business:services.service_description}}. The menu should describe each service in plain words, state the time it takes, and state any product the client should know about. It must not describe a result that the treatment cannot deliver, and it must never include an injectable treatment, which is excluded from this course.

instruction.heading: Add-ons that add value without adding risk
instruction.body: An add-on is a small extra service sold with a main treatment, such as a hand treatment with a nail service. Add-ons are useful because they raise the revenue from each visit without adding travel. The risk is that an add-on may need its own patch test, its own processing time or its own consent. A tinting add-on, for example, needs the product's patch test and the processing time from its label, as “Client consent, patch testing and contraindications” explains. An add-on should be checked for the same steps as the main service, and it should be recorded on the job record so that the materials cost is included in the price. The rule is that an add-on may not shorten a required step, and may not be offered as a replacement for the consent or the intake.

instruction.heading: Packages and the record they create
instruction.body: A package is a set of visits sold together at a set price. Packages are useful for clients who return regularly, but they create a record that the business must keep. The package should state the services included, the number of visits, the period it covers, and what happens if the client does not use all the visits. The package record must link each visit to the services delivered, and each visit must have its own intake and consent record, because a client's health can change between visits. The package terms are set in {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}.

procedure: Check every menu item against the approved service list, and remove any item that is not on it
Confirm that no injectable treatment appears on the menu or in any add-on
Check the time, product and steps for each add-on, including patch test and processing time
Write the package terms, including the services, visit count, period and expiry rule as the business has approved them
Record each visit in the package with its own intake and consent record
Review the menu and packages when the approved list, the products or the local rules change

workedExamples.situation: A therapist wants to add a 'skin rejuvenation' item to the menu that uses a chemical peel she has been trained on, and says it is a popular item in salons.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the item go on the menu this month?
workedExamples.reasoning: The item is not on the approved list, so it cannot go on the menu. The therapist should ask the business to review the scope, check the state and council position, and confirm the product's instructions before the item is added. A salon's popularity is not a reason to offer it.

workedExamples.situation: A client wants a bundle of six visits for a full nail service, with a hand treatment added to each visit at no extra charge.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should be checked before the bundle is offered?
workedExamples.reasoning: The bundle must list the services and the visit count, and each visit must have its own intake and consent record. The hand treatment must be on the approved list and must have its product checked, including any patch test. The price must cover the materials cost of each visit.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved service list and menu document with a review date
Package terms document, approved by the business
Intake and consent form for each visit within a package
Product safety data sheets for each product named on the menu

commonErrors.error: Adding a service to the menu because a salon offers it.
commonErrors.prevention: Only approved services go on the menu. Check the state and council position first.

commonErrors.error: Offering an add-on that shortens a processing time or skips a patch test.
commonErrors.prevention: Check every add-on for its own steps, and build the time and test into the booking.

commonErrors.error: Selling a package with no record of each visit.
commonErrors.prevention: Record each visit with its own intake, consent and services delivered.

commonErrors.error: Stating that a package cannot expire or must be refunded by law.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the package terms as the business policy.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The menu is a statement of scope. Items must be on the approved list and inside the state and council position recorded in “Mobile beauty scope and skin-treatment boundaries”, including the Victorian registrable services list (page updated 22 May 2026).
Injectable treatments are excluded from this course and must not appear on the menu or in any add-on.
Consumer-law rules for packages, refunds and expiry were not researched.
A menu, an add-on or a package does not register the business or grant any licence.

qualityStandard: Every menu item is on the approved service list, with a review date
No menu item or add-on includes an injectable treatment
Every add-on has its own steps, time and patch test check recorded
Every visit in a package has its own intake and consent record
documentationEvidence: Approved menu with the review date and the source for each item
Add-on review record showing the steps, time and test checked
Package terms signed or acknowledged by the client
Visit record for each package visit, linked to the package
summary: The menu is the scope, so only approved services go on it
An add-on must not shorten a step or replace consent and intake
Completing this lesson does not approve any service or grant any licence

knowledgeChecks.question: A salon offers a chemical peel that is popular with its clients. What is the correct status for adding it to a mobile menu under this course?
options: Add it, because salons offer it and clients ask for it on almost every booking at the front desk
Add it at a lower price to test demand, since a discount shows whether clients will book it at all in the first month
Hold it until the business has reviewed the scope, the state and council position, and the product instructions

knowledgeChecks.question: An add-on is tinting, which needs a patch test under its product instructions. What should the therapist do?
options: Carry out the test as the product instructions state, and record it with the add-on
Skip the test to keep the add-on price low, since the main service is already tested
Test the main service only, and apply the add-on without a separate patch test today

knowledgeChecks.question: Under this lesson, what must each visit in a package have?
options: One intake and consent record kept for the whole package
Its own intake and consent record
No record, because the package price is fixed
A record only if the client asks for one
